accroche: What tells you about a child is not his distress when the parent leaves. It is what he does on the parent's return.
contenu_vulgarise:
A one-year-old child, his mother, a room with toys, and a stranger. The protocol runs through eight short episodes: the mother leaves, the stranger stays; the mother returns; both leave; the mother returns again.

Mary Ainsworth developed this procedure in the late 1960s. What she observes is not the distress during the separation (almost all children protest). It is what happens at the reunion.

## Three Ways of Coming Back

Most children seek contact, let themselves be soothed, then go back to playing. Ainsworth speaks of secure attachment: the attachment figure works as a base, from which one moves away to explore and to which one returns for reassurance.

Others avoid contact on the return, staying turned toward the toys, looking indifferent. Their heart rate, however, indicates strong arousal. The indifference is a strategy, not an absence of emotion.

Still others are inconsolable: they demand contact and push it away at the same time, and take a long time to return to play.

A fourth category was added in 1990 by Mary Main and Judith Solomon: the so-called disorganized children, whose reactions on the return are contradictory or frozen, with no coherent strategy. It is today the most studied in clinical settings.

These responses are not temperaments. They match what the child has learned to expect: an adult who is available, distant, or unpredictable.

## What Has Been Revised

Ainsworth's work extends that of John Bowlby, whose first formulations assigned an almost exclusive role to the mother. The data did not confirm this: a child develops distinct attachments with several figures, and the quality of each depends on the relationship in question, not on a single, privileged bond.

Stability over time has also been revised downward. The classification observed at age one predicts less than had been hoped; later relationships weigh heavily, including family difficulties and the encounters that repair.

## What This Shifts

What remains, and is solid, is the notion of a secure base. One explores all the farther for knowing where to return. The bond is not what holds exploration back. It is what makes it possible.

The idea has spread well beyond early childhood (the study of adult bonds, grief work), all the way to management vocabulary. With the usual risk: the farther a notion travels from its data, the more it is impoverished.

repere.texte: Children who avoid contact on the return seem indifferent, but their heart rate indicates strong arousal: the avoidance is a strategy, not an absence of emotion.
repere.source: Ainsworth, Blehar, Waters & Wall, Patterns of Attachment (1978)

carte.punch: What matters is not the separation. It is what happens on the return.
carte.idee: Almost all children protest when the parent leaves. What Ainsworth observes is the moment of reunion: seeking contact, avoiding it, or demanding it without being soothed. Three responses matched to what the child has learned to expect.
carte.source_courte: Ainsworth et al., Patterns of Attachment, 1978

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full protocol and the episode-by-episode observation tables.

quiz.question: What exactly does Ainsworth's Strange Situation observe?
choix: The intensity of the child's distress at the moment the parent leaves the room
The child's ability to play alone in the presence of an unfamiliar person
The child's behavior at the reunion with the attachment figure
How long the child agrees to stay away from his parent
quiz.explication: Almost all children protest when the parent leaves: distress distinguishes nothing. It is the return that is informative: seeking contact and calming down, avoiding it in appearance, or demanding it without managing to calm down. These responses reflect what the child has learned to expect, not his temperament.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who added, in 1990, the fourth attachment category known as disorganized?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The disorganized category, the most studied in clinical settings today, was added in 1990 by Mary Main and Judith Solomon, completing the three styles described by Ainsworth.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did later data lead researchers to revise in John Bowlby's first formulations?
choix: The almost exclusive role assigned to the mother as the only attachment figure
The very existence of an attachment bond in the young child
The age at which the first attachment figure appears
The usefulness of the protocol for observing attachment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bowlby assigned an almost exclusive role to the mother. The data show that a child develops distinct attachments with several figures, each depending on the relationship in question.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the notion of a secure base mean, the idea that remains the most solid according to the entry?
choix: A secure child explores less than the others, out of caution
A child attaches to only one person at a time, never several
A secure child never protests when his parent leaves the room
A child explores all the farther for knowing whom to return to for reassurance
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The bond is not what holds exploration back but what makes it possible: the more reliable the secure base, the farther the child ventures before returning for reassurance.
